questions.q: If the function $f(x)=2 x^{3}-9 a x^{2}+12 a^{2} x+1$ attains its maximum and minimum at $p$ and $q$ respectively such that $p^{2}=q$, then $a$ equals
questions.solution: Given, $f(x)=2 x^{3}-9 a x^{2}+12 a^{2} x+1$ attains maximum and minimum at $p$ and $q$ respectively. $\therefore$ f^{\prime}(p)=0, f^{\prime}(q)=0 Now, $\begin{array}{c}$f^{\prime \prime}(p) < 0 \text { and } f^{\prime \prime}(q)>0 \\ f^{\prime}(p)=0 \end{array} and $\begin{array}{r}$f^{\prime}(q)=0 \\ 6 p^{2}-18 a p+12 a^{2}=0 \\ 6 q^{2}-18 a q+12 a^{2}=0 \end{array} and $\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow$& p^{2}-3 a p+2 a^{2}=0 \\ $\text { and }$& q^{2}-3 a q+2 a^{2}=0 \end{array} $p=a, 2 a, q=a, 2 a\begin{array}{lrl}\Rightarrow & p=a, 2 a, q=a, \\ \text { Now, } & f^{\prime \prime}(p) < 0\end{array} $\Rightarrow \quad 12 p-18 a < 0\Rightarrow \quad p < \frac{3}{2} a$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(q)>0 \Rightarrow 12 q-18 a>0\Rightarrow \quad q>$\frac{3}{2}$a$ From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get \begin{aligned}$p &=a, q=2 a \\ $\text { Now, } \quad$p^{2} &=q \end{aligned}$ \begin{array}{lc} \Rightarrow & a^{2}=2 a \\ \Rightarrow & a=0,2 \end{array} But for $a=0, f(x)=2 x^{3}+1$ which does not attains a maximum or minimum for any value of $x$. Hence, $a=2$. $

questions.q: The maximum area of the rectangle that can be inscribed in a circle of radius $r$, is
questions.solution: Area of rectangle, $\begin{aligned}$A &=2 x $\cdot$2 $\sqrt{r^{2}-x^{2}}$\\ &=4 x $\sqrt{r^{2}-x^{2}}$\\ $\frac{d A}{d x}$&=$\frac{4\left(r^{2}-2 x^{2}\right)}{\sqrt{r^{2}-x^{2}}} \end{aligned}$For maximum or minimum put $\frac{d A}{d x}=0$ \Rightarrow \quad x=r / $\sqrt{2}$It can be easily checked that $\frac{d^{2} A}{d x^{2}} < 0$ for this value of $x$. $\therefore A$ is maximum for $x=\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}$ and the maximum value of $A$ is given by A=4 $\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{r^{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2}}=$2 r^{2}

questions.solution: Let $f(x)=x^{3}-12 x^{2}+36 x+17\therefore f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^{2}-24 x+36=0$ For maxima, put $f^{\prime}(x)=0\Rightarrow \quad 3 x^{2}-24 x+36=0\Rightarrow \quad(x-2)(x-6)=0\Rightarrow \quad x=2,6$ Again, $f^{\prime \prime}(x)=6 x-24$ is negative at $x=2$ So that, $f(6)=17, f(2)=49$ At the end points, $f(1)=42, f(10)=177$ So that, $f(x)$ has its maximum value 177 .

questions.q: If $\mathrm{f}(x)=x \mathrme^{x(1-x)}, x \in \mathrm{R}$, then $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{f}($x) & =x \mathrme^{x(1-x)} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrmf^{\prime}(x) & =x \mathrme^{x(1-x)}[x(-1)+(1-x)]+\mathrme^{x(1-x)} \\ & =\mathrme^{x(1-x)}\left($x-2 x²+1\right) \end{aligned} For $\mathrm{f}(x)$ to be increasing, $\mathrmf^{\prime}(x) \geq 0\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \mathrme^{x(1-x)}\left($x-2 x²+1\right) \geq 0 \\ & \Rightarrow x-2 x²+1 \geq 0 \\ & \Rightarrow 2 x²-x-1 \leq 0 \\ & \Rightarrow(2 x+1)(x-1) \leq 0 \\ & \Rightarrow x \in\left[-\frac{1}{2},$1\right] \end{aligned} For $\mathrm{f}(x)$ to be decreasing, $\mathrmf^{\prime}(x) \leq 0\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } \Rightarrow(2 x+1)(x-1) \geq 0 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow x \in\left(-\infty,-\frac{1}{2}\right] \cup[$1, $\infty) \end{aligned}$

questions.q: On the interval $[0,1]$ the function $x^{25}(1-x)^{75}$ takes its maximum value at the point
questions.solution: Given, $f(x)=x^{25}(1-x)^{75}$ \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x) &=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{75}-75 x^{25}(1-x)^{74} \\ &=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x) \\ \therefore \quad f^{\prime}(x) &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=0,1,1 / 4 \end{aligned} If $x < 1 / 4$, then f^{\prime}(x)=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x)>0 . and if $x>1 / 4$, then f^{\prime}(x)=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x) < 0 . Thus, $f^{\prime}(x)$ changes its sign from positive to negative as $x$ passes through $1 / 4$ from left to right. Hence, $f(x)$ attains its maximum at $x=1 / 4$.

questions.q: In a triangle, the sum of lengths of two sides is $x$ and the product of the lengths of the same two sides is $y$. If $x^2-\mathrm{c}^2-y$, where $\mathrm{c}$ is the length of the third side of the triangle, then the circumradius of the triangle is
questions.solution: Let $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$ be the lengths of two sides of $\mathrm{a}$ triangle. $\therefore \quad$ According to the given condition, $\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=$x $\text { and } \mathrm{ab}=$y \\ & \therefore \quad x²-$\mathrm{c}^2=y \Rightarrow($\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})^2-$\mathrm{c}^2=$\mathrm{ab}$\\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow a²+b²+2 a b-c²=a b \\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow a²+b²-c²=-a b \\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow $\frac{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2-\mathrm{c}^2}{2 \mathrm{ab}}=-\frac{1}{2}$\\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow \cos $\mathrm{C}=\frac{1}{2}$\\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow $\mathrm{C}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$\\  \text{ and }  \Rightarrow $\text { circumradius }=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{2 \sin \mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{2 \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\sqrt{3}}\\ & \end{aligned}

differentiating w.r.t. $t$ both side

questions.q: A kite is $120 \mathrm{~m}$ high and $130 \mathrm{~m}$ of string is out. If the kite is moving away horizontally at the rate of $39 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm\sec$, then the rate at which the string is being out, is
questions.solution: Let 'P' be the position of the kite and PR be the string. Let $\mathrm{QR}=x$ and $\mathrm{PR}=y$ By Pythagoras theorem, $\begin{aligned} & -\mathrm{PR}^2=\mathrm{PQ}^2+\mathrm{QR}^2 \\ & \Rightarrow y^2=(120)^2+x^2... (i) \end{aligned}$ Differentiating w.r.t.t, we get $\begin{aligned} & 2 y \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{dt}}=2 x \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \Rightarrow y \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{dt}}=x \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}}... (ii) \end{aligned}$ Now, kite is moving away horizontally at the rate of $39 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm\sec$. $\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}}=39 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm\sec \\ & \text { From (i), } \\ & (130)^2=(120)^2+x^2 \\ \Rightarrow & x^2=16900-14400 \\ \Rightarrow & x^2=2500 \\ \Rightarrow & x=50 \\ & \text { From (ii), } \\ & 130 \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{dt}}=50 \times 39 \\ \therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{50 \times 39}{130}=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm\sec \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The maximum value of $x^4 y^4$ when $a^2 x^4+b^2 y^4=c^6$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text {Let } f(x)=x^4 y^4 \\ & \text { And } a^2 x^4+b^2 y^4=c^6 \\ & \Rightarrow y^4=\frac{1}{b^2}\left(c^6-a^2 x^4\right) \\ & \therefore \quad f(x)=\mathrm{x}^4 \cdot \frac{1}{b^2}\left(c^6-a^2 x^4\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{b^2} x^4\left(c^6-a^2 x^4\right) \\ & f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{b^2}\left(4 x^{3 c^6}-8 a^2 x^7\right) \\ & \end{aligned}$ for extrem point: $\begin{aligned} & f^{\prime}(\mathrm{x})=0 \Rightarrow 4 x^3\left(c^6-2 a^2 x^4\right)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x=0 \text { or } x^4=\frac{c^6}{2 a^2} \end{aligned}$ For maxima : $x=\frac{c^6}{2 a^2}\therefore$ The maximum value is : $\begin{aligned} & f\left(x=\left(\frac{c^6}{2 a^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}\right) \\ & =\frac{c^6}{2 a^2} \cdot \frac{1}{b^2}\left[c^6-a^2 \cdot \frac{c^6}{2 a^2}\right] \\ & =\frac{c^6}{2 a^2 b^2} \cdot \frac{c^6}{2}=\frac{c^{12}}{4 a^2 b^2} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: Find the minimum value of $2x + 3y$ when $xy = 6$.
questions.solution:
Given:& $xy = 6$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{6}{x}$

$⇒ f\left(x, y\right) = 2x + 3y$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 2x + 3 \times \dfrac{6}{x}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 2x + \dfrac{18}{x}$

$⇒ f^{'}\left(x\right) = 2 - \dfrac{18}{x2}$

Put~$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$~for maximum or minimum

$⇒ 0 = 2 - \dfrac{18}{x2}$

$⇒ x^{2} = 9$

$⇒ x = \pm 3$

$⇒ f^{''} \left(x\right) = 0 - \left(\dfrac{- 18 \times 2}{x3}\right)

$⇒ f^{''} \left($3\right) = $\dfrac{36}{33}$> 0$

$⇒ f^{''} ( 3 ) > 0$

At~$x = 3, f\left($x\right)$~is minimum

The minimum value of~$f\left($3\right) = 2\left($3\right) + 3\left($2\right) = 12.

$

questions.solution: $\because f^{\prime}(x)=3 p x^2+2 q x+r$ ...(i) Since, $f(x)$ attain local minimum and maximum at $x=-2$ and $x=2$ respectively. $\therefore f^{\prime}(x)=k(x+2)(x-2)=k  \left(x^2-4\right)$ ...(ii) From (i) and (ii) \begin{aligned}$& k\left(x^2-4\right)=3 p x^2+2 q x+r \\ & \Rightarrow \quad k x^2-4 k=3 p x^2+2 q x+r\end{aligned}$ Comparing both sides, we get $k=3 p, q=0$ and $r=-4 k$ Now, $f^{\prime \prime}(x)=6 p x+2 q=6 p x \quad\{\because q=0\}\Rightarrow f^{\prime \prime}(-2)=-12 p>0 \quad\{\because x=-2$ is local minimum $\}\Rightarrow p < 0\because p$ is a root of $9 x^2-1=0 \Rightarrow x= \pm $\frac{1}{3}\therefore$p < 0 \Rightarrow $p=-\frac{1}{3} So, $k=3 \times\$left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)=-$1\Rightarrow r=-4 k=-4(-1)=4\therefore $p+q+r=-\f$frac{1}{3}+0+4=\frac{11}{3}.$

questions.q: A ladder of length $17 \mathrm{~m}$ rests with one end against a vertical wall and the other on the level ground. If the lower end slips away at the rate of $1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm\sec$., then when it is $8 \mathrm{~m}$ away from the wall, its upper end is coming down at the rate of
questions.solution: In $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \mathrm{AC}$ represents ladder $\mathrm{AB} \rightarrow$ vertical wall Let $\mathrm{AB}=x, \mathrm{BC}=y\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{ABC}=90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$ By Pythagoras theorem, $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{AB}^2+\mathrm{BC}^2=\mathrm{AC}^2 \\ & \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=17^2 \\ & \Rightarrow x^2=289-y^2 ... (i)\\ & \Rightarrow x^2=289-64 \\ & \Rightarrow x^2=225 \\ & \Rightarrow x=15 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$ Consider equation (i), $x^2=289-y^2$ Differentiating w.r.t. t, we get $\begin{aligned} & 2 x \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}}=-2 y \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \Rightarrow 15 \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}}=-8(1) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{-8}{15} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$ Negative sign shows that the ladder is moving down. i.e., vertical length is decreasing $\therefore \quad$ Upper end is coming down at the rate of $\frac{8}{15} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

questions.q: If $\log (1+x)-\frac{2 x}{2+x}$ is increasing, then
questions.solution:
Let $f(x)=\log (1+x)-\frac{2 x}{2+x^2}$
f^{\prime}(x)=$\frac{1}{(1+x)}-\frac{2}{2+x}+\frac{2 x}{(2+x)^2}$For increasing function, $f^{\prime}(x)>0\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad($2+x)^2-2(2+x)(1+x)+2 x(1+x) & >0 \\
\Rightarrow 4+x²+4 x-4-6 x-2 x²+2 x+2 x² & >0 \\
x² & >0

questions.q: If $\theta$ is the acute angle between the curves $x^2+y^2=4$ and $y^2=3 x$ then $\tan \theta=$
questions.solution: Given curves are $x^2+y^2=4$ and $y^2=3 x$ Put the value of $y^2$. $\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow x²+3 x-4=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x²+4 x-x-4=0 \\ & x(x+4)-1(x+4)=0 \\ & (x-1)(x+4)=0 \\ & x-1=0, x+4=0 \\ & x=1, x=-4 \end{aligned} Put in $y^2=3 \mathrm{x}$, then, $y^2=3, y= \pm \sqrt{3}$. $(x, y) \rightarrow(1, \sqrt{3}) \ \text{ and } (1, \sqrt{3})$ Now, Differentiate both curves w.r.t $x\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow x²+y²=4 \\ & 2 x+2 y $\cdot \frac{d y}{d x}=$0 \\ & y $\frac{d y}{d x}=-$x \\ & $\frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{x}{y}$\\ & \Rightarrow y=$\sqrt{3 x}$\\ & $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 \sqrt{x}} \end{aligned}$Put the point $(1, \sqrt{3})$ in their differentiation. $\begin{aligned}$& m_1=$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}},$m_2=$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$\\ & \tan $\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1 m_2}\right|=\left|\frac{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\right|=\left|\frac{\frac{-2-3}{2 \sqrt{3}}}{\frac{1}{2}}\right|$\\ & \tan $\theta=\left|\frac{-5}{\sqrt{3}}\right|=\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$So, $\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}$ is the correct option.

questions.q: If $f:[2,3] \rightarrow R$ is defined by $f(x)=x^3+3 x-2$, then the range $f(x)$ is contained in the interval
questions.solution:
Given, $f(x)=x^3+3 x-2$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& \quad f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^2+3 \\
& \text { Put } \quad f^{\prime}(x)=0 \Rightarrow 3 x^2+3=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad x^2=-1 \\
& \therefore \quad f(x) \text { is either increasing or decreasing. } \\
& \text { At } x=2, f(2)=2^3+3(2)-2=12 \\
& \text { At } x=3, f(3)=3^3+3(3)-2=34 \\
& \therefore f(x) \in[12,34] .
\end{aligned}$

and ${\text{f} ⁡}^{′} \left(2\right) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + 4 \beta + 1 = 0$

Adding,

$- \dfrac{3 \alpha}{2} + 3 = 0$

$∴ \alpha = 2$

questions.q: On which of the following intervals is the function $x^{100} + sinx - 1$ decreasing?
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = x^{100} + sinx - 1$

$⇒ f^{′} \left(x\right) = 100x^{99} + cosx$

If $0 < x < \dfrac{π}{2} ,$ then $f^{′} \left(x\right) > 0,$ , therefore $f\left(x\right)$ is increasing on \left(0, $\dfrac{π}{2}\right) .

If $0 < x < 1,$ then

$100x^{99} > 0$ and $cosx > 0$ [$∵ x$ lies between $0$ and $1$ ]

$⇒ f^{′} \left(x\right) = 100x^{99} + cosx > 0$

$⇒ f\left(x\right)$ is increasing on \left(0, 1\right) .$

If $\dfrac{π}{2}< x < \pi,$then

$100x^{99} > 100 \left[∵ x > 1 ⇒ x^{99} > 1\right]$

$⇒ 100x^{99} + cosx > 0 \left[$∵ cosx $\ge -$1 ⇒ 100x^{99} + cosx > 99\right]$

$⇒ f^{′} \left($x\right) > 0 ⇒ f \left(x\right)$ is increasing in \left(\dfrac{π}{2} , \pi\right) .$

questions.q: $f\left(x\right) = - 1 + kx + k$ neither touches nor intercepts the curve $f\left(x\right) = ln ⁡ x$, then minimum value of $k \in$& is
questions.solution:
$f \left(x\right) = - 1 + kx + k$

$f\left(x\right)$~represents straight line with slope~$k$~and $y$-intercept~ \left(k - 1\right)$.

$f \left(x\right) + 1 = k \left($x + 1\right)$

So for all values of~$k$, it always passes through~ \left(-1, - 1\right)$

For minimum slope of line, it will be touching the curve~$y = lnx$

When two curves touches, then at the common point their slopes are equal.

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = k$~,~$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{x}$

$k = \dfrac{1}{x}⇒ x = \dfrac{1}{k},y = ln\dfrac{1}{k}$

common point~$⇒ $\$left(\dfrac{1}{k}, -lnk\right)$

Slope of line can be written from two points on the line.$\dfrac{- lnk - \left(-$1\$r$rright)}{\dfrac{1}{k} -\left(-$1\right)} = k$

$1 - lnk = $k\$left(\dfrac{1}{k} +1\right)$

$= 1 + k$

$lnk + k = 0$

For solution of above equation, consider~f\left($k\right) = lnk + k$

f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) =ln \$left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) + \dfrac{1}{e} = \dfrac{1}{e} -$1$

$f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right)< 0$

$f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) = ln\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) + \dfrac{1}{e} = \dfrac{1}{e} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2 - \sqrt{e}}{2\sqrt{e}}$

$f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) > 0$

So~$f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) \cdot f\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right) < 0$

So atleast one root lies between~$\dfrac{1}{e}$and~$\dfrac{1}{e}$.

Hence,~$k \in \left(\dfrac{1}{e}, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$

For~$1 0$

and~\dfrac{1 - \log_{\mathrm{e}}x}{x2}$> 0in \left(1,e\right)$

and~$\dfrac{1 - \log_{\mathrm{e}}x}{x2} < 0in \left($e, $\infty\right)

Hence, $f ( x )$ is increasing in $( 1, e )$ and decreasing in $( e, \infty ).$
